title: Driving in Albania: Rules, Road Conditions and Practical Tips for Tourists
metaTitle: Driving in Albania: Rules, Roads & Safety Tips
metaDescription: Driving in Albania explained: road rules, speed limits, mountain roads, police checks, parking, fuel and tolls. Practical tips before you pick up your car.
excerpt: Is driving in Albania safe and what should you expect? Road rules, speed limits, mountain roads, parking, fuel, tolls and the local driving style, explained for visitors.
keywords: is it safe to drive in Albania
html:
Driving in Albania is very manageable for visitors: the main roads between Tirana, Durrës, Vlorë and the south are in good condition, signs use the Latin alphabet, and Albania drives on the right like the rest of continental Europe. What takes getting used to is the local driving style, the narrow mountain roads and the occasional surprise, such as a flock of sheep around a bend. This guide covers the rules, road conditions and practical habits that will make your trip relaxed and safe.

Is it safe to drive in Albania?

Yes, for a careful and alert driver. Road infrastructure has improved a lot in recent years, and most tourist routes are paved. The main risks come from other drivers' habits, such as sudden overtaking, unexpected stops and drivers not signalling, and from unlit rural roads at night. Drive defensively, keep a safe distance and assume others may not follow the rules, and you will be fine.

Basic rules of the road

  • Drive on the right and overtake on the left.
  • Seat belts are mandatory for everyone in the car, front and back.
  • Children should travel in a suitable child seat. Rent Ride can add child seats to your booking.
  • No phone in your hand while driving. Use a hands-free mount for navigation.
  • Drink-driving rules are strict. The simplest and safest rule is not to drink at all if you are driving.
  • Carry your documents: driving licence, passport or ID, and the rental agreement.

Speed limits

Limits are generally 40 km/h in towns, 80 km/h on open roads and 110 km/h on motorways, but signposted limits change often, especially near villages, junctions and roadworks. Always follow the signs. Speed cameras and police radar checks are common on main roads, including the routes between Tirana, Durrës and Vlorë.

Roundabouts

Albania has many roundabouts, particularly in Tirana and on the approach roads to larger towns. In general you give way to traffic already on the roundabout, but local drivers do not always behave predictably. Enter slowly, watch cars on both sides and do not assume an indicator means what it says.

Road conditions: what to expect

Motorways and main roads

The key routes are good: the dual carriageway from Tirana to Durrës, the road south through Fier towards Vlorë, and the Rruga e Kombit (the Nation's Road) from Milot towards Kukës and the Kosovo border. Expect occasional roadworks and slower stretches through towns, where roads pass straight through village centres.

Coastal and mountain roads

The Riviera road south of Vlorë climbs over the Llogara Pass and then twists along the coast through Dhërmi, Himarë and Borsh. It is paved and spectacular, but narrow in places with tight hairpins and steep drops. In the mountains of the north, roads such as the route from Shkodër to Theth are now paved but remain slow, winding and in places single-lane. Plan for low average speeds: 40 km in the mountains can easily take an hour.

Rural roads and beach access

Side roads to some beaches and villages can be gravel, with potholes and steep sections. If your itinerary includes remote areas, consider an SUV rental for better ground clearance.

The local driving style

Albanian drivers tend to be assertive. A few things you are likely to see:

  • Short honks are often a friendly "I'm here" before a blind bend or when overtaking, not aggression.
  • Overtaking can happen on bends or with little space. Stay to the right and let faster drivers pass.
  • Sudden stops to pick someone up, buy fruit at a roadside stall or chat with a friend.
  • Pedestrians and animals on the road, especially in villages and in the countryside. Cows, sheep and goats are common on mountain roads.
  • Double parking in towns, which can narrow a street to one lane.

The best approach is calm, predictable driving and keeping more distance than you would at home.

Police checks

Police checkpoints are a normal part of driving in Albania, often at the entrance to towns or on main roads. If you are waved over, stop, stay polite and show your licence, passport and the rental documents. Officers often just check papers and let tourists continue. Never offer money. Keep your documents somewhere easy to reach, such as the glove box.

Tolls

Most Albanian roads are free to use. The best-known toll road is the Rruga e Kombit (Milot to Morinë, towards Kosovo), with a toll station on the route. Payment is at the booth. If you are heading to Kosovo, read our guide to crossing borders with a rental car first, as you need a cross-border permit for the car.

Fuel

  • Petrol stations are frequent along main roads and around towns, and many are open late.
  • In mountain areas, stations are far apart, so fill up before you head into the hills.
  • Many stations accept cards, but carry some cash in Albanian lek for smaller stations, parking and roadside cafés.
  • Check whether your car takes petrol or diesel before you fill up. It is shown in your rental agreement and usually on the fuel cap.
  • Rental cars are handed over full and should be returned full.

Parking

Parking is the biggest daily challenge, mainly in Tirana and in the coastal towns in summer.

  • Tirana: street parking in the centre is limited. Use paid car parks or hotel parking where possible.
  • Old towns such as Berat and Gjirokastër have steep, narrow cobbled lanes. Park lower down and walk up.
  • Beach towns in July and August: expect paid parking lots near the beach and arrive early.
  • Never block driveways or park on pavements, as towing and fines do happen.
  • Do not leave valuables visible in the car.

Driving at night

Where possible, avoid long drives after dark, especially on mountain and rural roads. Many roads are unlit, road markings can be faded, and you may meet pedestrians, cyclists without lights or animals on the road. Plan your days so you arrive before sunset, particularly on routes like the Llogara Pass or the road to Theth.

Navigation and connectivity

Google Maps and similar apps work well on main routes, but their time estimates can be optimistic on mountain roads. Download offline maps before you head into areas with weak signal, such as the Albanian Alps. A GPS unit can be added to your rental if you prefer not to use your phone.

If something goes wrong

In case of an accident, stop safely, turn on your hazard lights, put on the safety vest and set up the warning triangle. Call the police (129) if anyone is injured or if there is damage involving another vehicle, and contact Rent Ride's 24/7 support on +355 69 81 45 803 (phone or WhatsApp). Do not move the cars or sign anything you do not understand before speaking to us. A police report is usually needed for insurance purposes.

Choosing the right car for Albanian roads

For cities and the main coastal road, a compact car is easy to park and economical. For families, mountain areas and gravel access roads, an SUV is more comfortable. If you are not confident with hill starts, an automatic car makes steep old towns and mountain roads much easier. Whatever you choose, adding Super CDW removes the excess and gives you peace of mind on narrow roads.

faq.question: Can I drive in Albania with my EU or UK driving licence?
faq.answer: EU and most other international driving licences are accepted for renting and driving a car in Albania. For Rent Ride you must have held your licence for at least one year. If your licence is not printed in the Latin alphabet, contact us before travelling to check whether you should also carry an International Driving Permit.

faq.question: Which side of the road do they drive on in Albania?
faq.answer: Albania drives on the right-hand side of the road, and you overtake on the left, as in Germany, Italy, France and most of continental Europe. Rental cars have the steering wheel on the left. Visitors from the UK should take extra care at roundabouts and when pulling out of junctions during the first days.

faq.question: Are there toll roads in Albania?
faq.answer: Most roads in Albania are free. The main toll road travellers meet is the Rruga e Kombit motorway between Milot and Morinë, which leads towards Kosovo and has a toll station on the route. Payment is made at the booth. Driving within the country to the coast or the south generally involves no tolls.

faq.question: Is it safe to drive at night in Albania?
faq.answer: Main roads near Tirana are fine at night, but rural and mountain roads are often unlit, with faded markings, pedestrians and animals on the road. For safety, plan longer drives such as the Llogara Pass or the road to Theth in daylight and aim to arrive before sunset.

faq.question: What should I do if the police stop me in Albania?
faq.answer: Police checks are routine. Pull over safely, stay calm and polite, and show your driving licence, passport or ID and the rental documents. In most cases officers simply check the papers and let you continue. Keep the documents in the glove box so they are easy to reach.
